thread.title: The No. 1 Stock In The World (Redux) - Part 3

author: Mike Nadel
title: The No. 1 Stock In The World (Redux) - Part 3
text:
Three years ago, I asked a panel of Seeking Alpha regulars to take part in the audacious exercise of choosing the best stock in the world.
The three-part series that came out of it ( Part 1 , Part 2 , Part 3 ) turned out to be such a hit with readers that I wanted to do an updated version of the collaborative project.
As unlikely as it seems, the panelists actually outdid themselves with their answers for the following two questions:
1. If you could only own one company in your portfolio and you were buying it today, which would it be? Why?
2. If you had $25,000 to invest TODAY on one company and you planned to hold it for 10 years or more, which company would you buy? Why?
The only rule I gave the panelists was that they had to choose one common stock (as opposed to an ETF, mutual fund or preferred stock) for each scenario.
Here is a recap of their selections, with answers to Question 1 listed first, followed by their Question 2 choices:
Adam Aloisi: Honeywell ( HON ); Nutanix ( NTNX ). Ian Bezek: McCormick ( MKC ); Grupo Aeroportuario del Pacifico ( PAC ) Buyandhold 2012: Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ); UnitedHealth Group ( UNH ). Dividend Sensei: Brookfield Infrastructure Partners ( BIP ); Enbridge ( ENB ) - via Spectra Energy Partners ( SEP ). Eddie Herring: Coca-Cola ( KO ); Apple ( AAPL ). kolpin: Johnson & Johnson; Becton, Dickinson ( BDX ) Eric Landis: Altria ( MO ); Visa ( V ). Paul Leibowitz: Johnson & Johnson - both questions. Julian Lin: Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG ) ( GOOGL ) - both questions. RoseNose: AT&T ( T ); AbbVie ( ABBV ). scoots: Alphabet; Tencent ( OTCPK:TCEHY ). ScottU: Altria; Visa. Nicholas Ward: Johnson & Johnson; Apple. OK, folks ... now it's my turn.
I made my selections before I received the panelists' responses ... and I'm glad, because it would have been easy to be influenced by their persuasive arguments.
For Question 1: Alphabet
(Graphic from google.com)
My other finalists included Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRK.A ) ( BRK.B ), Lockheed Martin ( LMT ), Mastercard ( MA ), Philip Morris ( PM ) and Visa. BRK because of its scope, diversity and management; LMT because the world is always bullish on war machines; MA and V because they are two of my favorite growth companies; and PM because it has gotten beaten up too badly.
My interpretation of Question 1 led me to select a fundamentally sound industry leader that is valued at least decently relative to its own historic metrics. It would be the only company in my portfolio, but there's no requirement to hold it for years (or even months).
Having said that, I am a buy-and-holdish guy and a very reluctant seller. Knowing that about myself - and I think it is crucial for each investor to know himself or herself - I went in planning to hold GOOGL for a very long time.
Maybe not for the 10 years as mandated by Question 2 ... but who knows? Maybe longer!
So, why Alphabet?
First, I have a thing for the dominant brand in any industry. It's why I own Visa and Nike ( NKE ) and McDonald's ( MCD ) and Johnson & Johnson and McCormick and Starbucks (NASDAQ: SBUX ) and Altria, among others.
You can't get away from Google if you try. That might frustrate those who would rather protect their privacy, but for an investor, it's quite appealing.
Second, while GOOGL isn't a screaming buy, it is fairly valued, as indicated in the following FAST Graphs illustrations - the top one showing current and historic P/E ratio, the bottom depicting current and historic P/FCF ratio.
I could go on and on about what makes Alphabet a great investment, but panelists Julian Lin and scoots did such a tremendous job in Part 1, I think it would be silly to repeat what they said. I highly recommend interested parties check out what they wrote.
As I am a Dividend Growth Investing proponent, some might wonder why I would choose a company that produces no income.
Hey, I know Question 1 is about a one-stock portfolio, and I selected GOOGL in good faith with that in mind. (I even bought a few shares so I would have skin in the game.) But to get into this no-dividend discussion, let's get real: Few investors own only one stock.
Let's say I have $2 million portfolio (A man can dream, right?). If I put $1.2 million into high-quality "DGI stocks" with a combined 3% yield, I have reasonable certainty that those investments will generate a $36K dividend stream that will increase over time. I could take another $500K and buy "growthier" companies like V, MA and, yes, GOOGL. As long as I am comfortable going in that I will have to sell shares if I need cash from those investments, I see no reason to exclude them. For added liquidity and safety, I might use the last $300K for conservative assets, notably bonds and cash.
If my income requirements are otherwise met, would I cease being a DGI practitioner because I bought a stock that doesn't produce dividends? I don't think so.
Besides, there's a fair chance that Alphabet will pay a substantial, growing dividend one day, just as AAPL and Microsoft ( MSFT ) do now.
Indeed, I just googled "will alphabet pay a dividend," and it showed that millions of inquiring minds want to know!
For Question 2: NextEra Energy ( NEE ) My other finalists were Johnson & Johnson, McCormick, Microsoft, Apple, Visa, Mastercard, McDonald's ( MCD ) and 3M ( MMM ). JNJ and MMM because they are successful, multi-industry conglomerates; MSFT and AAPL because they are old-school tech warriors that keep making big profits; MKC because it has been the classic defensive play while also offering growth; V and MA because they constitute a money-making duopoly; and MCD because people will eat cheap food regardless of how the economy is doing.
Due to the required 10-year holding period, I wanted a company that has performed relatively well through good markets and bad (and figures to keep doing so). I also wanted an industry leader with an outstanding dividend growth record (and realistic expectations for that to continue).
In less than 20 years, NextEra has grown from the nation's 30th-largest utility to numero uno in the world. Most of the same management team that led the charge is still in place.
Moreover, the company has become a world leader in renewable energy. That's a feel-good story for tree-huggers, sure, but it also has been highly profitable for NEE and its shareholders.
(Photograph from nexteraenergy.com)
A recent Wall Street Journal piece details the company's incredible surge. The article is behind a paywall, unavailable for non-subscribers, but here is the gist:
The Florida company has grown into a green Goliath, almost entirely under the radar, not through taking on heavy debt to expand or by touting its greenness, but by relentlessly capitalizing on government support for renewable energy, in particular the tax subsidies that help finance wind and solar projects around the country. It then sells the output to utilities, many of which must procure power from green sources to meet state mandates.
NextEra has been careful to build sites only after it has customers lined up, avoiding debt problems that sank rivals such as SunEdison Inc. And it has assiduously avoided the kind of claims of altruistic motives that are common among some green-energy companies.
“They were focused on business fundamentals and not the Hollywood status” that comes with being a champion of green power, said Andrew Hoffman, a University of Michigan business professor who was on a NextEra advisory board until 2012.
Just last month, NEE acquired Gulf Power, Florida City Gas, and two natural gas power plants. Not only will these assets grow NextEra's already impressive footprint, but as the following slide from this week's J.P. Morgan Energy Conference shows, the acquisitions will positively affect NEE's earnings.
EPS gains are nothing new for NEE. Since the dawn of this millennium, the company has grown earnings every single year - including through the dot-com bust, the Great Recession, Fed rate decisions, political upheavals, etc. (The red-circled area shows expected continued growth.)
NEE's growth story is one reason I'm comfortable buying it today and holding it for 10 years. And then there's this ...
That NEE suffered a significantly smaller drawdown than the S&P 500 Index ( SPY ) during the Great Recession is not exactly stunning, as utilities are defensive. But how about NextEra's total return besting SPY's during the current bull run? How about NEE topping SPY both over the last year and during 2018 so far? And how about NEE crushing its own industry benchmark, the Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF ( XLU ), in every time period? Wow!
(Data compiled using the DividendChannel.com calculator )
As impressive as that is, I know many of you all are DGI proponents looking to solidify your income streams. Well, NextEra's dividend has grown like a weed, too.
NEE Dividend data by YCharts
In February, NextEra announced a 13% increase , from $3.93 per share to $4.44. This continues a trend, as NEE’s average annual dividend growth is 11% over the last 5 years and 9% over the last 10.
And the beat will go on: NEE says it will raise divvies by 12% to 14% in 2019 and again in 2020. The '19 increase would mark the 25 th consecutive year of annual payout growth, making NextEra Energy a Dividend Aristocrat.
NEE's dividend yield of 2.7% is relatively low for utilities. It also is richly valued; it has a 20+ forward P/E ratio because, unlike most of its peers, it has had positive total return in 2018 despite Fed rate hikes and other headwinds.
NEE Total Return Price data by YCharts
If I have to hold a company for 10 years, I'm willing to give up a little current yield and pay a bit of a premium for a proven performer that seems poised to continue growing. All this while being in a defensive sector.
Before I finally bought NextEra last year, I knew it was a top utility. During the course of my research, I learned that the company was even better than I had thought.
Conclusion Obviously, there is no way to know today what really is the No. 1 stock in the world. I mean, Question 2 specifically demands that we wait a decade before concluding anything!
What this series has done is provide intriguing candidates for further research. Additionally, the panelists' insightful commentary about their selections has been extremely valuable; I can't thank those 13 Seeking Alphites enough. The comment streams have been great, too, filled with ideas and debate.
Thanks for reading, everybody, and for taking part in the discussion.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL, ABBV, HON, JNJ, KO, LMT, MA, MCD, MKC, MMM, MO, MSFT, NEE, PM, T, V, GOOGL.
